segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In 1989, film production in Britain was at a low ebb. Audience numbers were starting to grow, but few British films enjoyed commercial success. Yet the talent of British actors remained in evidence, and Daniel Day-Lewis (b. 1957) greeted the new decade by winning the Oscar for Best Actor for his performance as Christy Brown in My Left Foot: The Story of Christy Brown (1989).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Fifteen British and Irish actors received Oscar nominations for Best Actor or Actress in the 1990s, and their success kept Anglo-Irish cinema in the spotlight. The decade saw the passing of one of Britain's most innovative directors, Derek Jarman (1942-1994), but new talents burst onto the scene, such as Danny Boyle (b. 1956), with the wry Shallow Grave (1994) and Trainspotting (1996). Guy Ritchie (b. 1968) reinvigorated the gangster film with his black comedy about cockney criminals, Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels (1998).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Meanwhile, Mike Leigh (b. 1943) consolidated his position as a major director with three internationally acclaimed films - Life Is Sweet (1990), Naked (1993) and Secrets & Lies (1996). The last of these charted new territory by examining racial barriers and stereotypes, reflecting a contemporary Britain trying to integrate an increasingly multiethnic identity.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The British said goodbye to Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in 1990, but Anglo-Irish films continued to reflect her philosophy. Neil Jordan (b. 1950), with The Crying Game (1992), and Jim Sheridan (b. 1949), with In the Name of the Father (1993), explored the effects of the Irish question and gave the conflict a human face.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Sheridan's film was based on the true story of the Guildford Four, who were wrongly accused of taking part in an IRA pub bombing. Daniel Day-Lewis plays one of the accused, Gerry Conlon, and the story centers on his relationship with his father, Giuseppe (Pete Postlethwaite), who was also imprisoned, and with his lawyer, Gareth Peirce (Emma Thompson). The lead actors earned Oscar nominations for their performances - the rebellious son, the humble father and the fighting lawyer made the film deeply moving. Directed by Ken Loach (b. 1936), Land and Freedom (1995) explores similar themes of identity and idealism against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Although period dramas such as Howards End (1992) and Shakespeare in Love (1998) showed that they were still Britain's strong suit, the most gratifying development of the decade was the resurgence in popularity of homegrown comedy. The romantic comedy Four Weddings and a Funeral (1994), directed by Mike Newell (b. 1942), was a huge hit and launched the collaboration between screenwriter Richard Curtis (b. 1956) and actor Hugh Grant (b. 1960), which produced another hit five years later, Notting Hill (1999).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Grant's knack for portraying the bumbling but attractive middle-class bachelor struck a chord with audiences around the world, even if this English stereotype did not always seem familiar to local viewers. The success of Four Weddings and a Funeral paved the way for more authentic British productions such as Brassed Off (1996) and The Full Monty (1997), which showed working-class people who might be down but did not feel defeated.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The resistance of the brass band members in Brassed Off to the closure of their rehearsal space, and of the unemployed men in The Full Monty who become strippers, appealed to international audiences, showing that Anglo-Irish filmmakers did not need to dilute their own culture to suit American tastes.
